abstract: Accurate document layout analysis is a key requirement for high-quality PDF document conversion. With the recent availability of public, large ground-truth datasets such as PubLayNet and DocBank, deep-learning models have proven to be very effective at layout detection and segmentation. While these datasets are of adequate size to train such models, they severely lack in layout variability since they are sourced from scientific article repositories such as PubMed and arXiv only. Consequently, the accuracy of the layout segmentation drops significantly when these models are applied on more challenging and diverse layouts. In this paper, we present DocLayNet, a new, publicly available, document-layout annotation dataset in COCO format. It contains 80863 manually annotated pages from diverse data sources to represent a wide variability in layouts. For each PDF page, the layout annotations provide labelled bounding-boxes with a choice of 11 distinct classes. DocLayNet also provides a subset of double- and triple-annotated pages to determine the inter-annotator agreement. In multiple experiments, we provide baseline accuracy scores (in mAP) for a set of popular object detection models. We also demonstrate that these models fall approximately 10% behind the inter-annotator agreement. Furthermore, we provide evidence that DocLayNet is of sufficient size. Lastly, we compare models trained on PubLayNet, DocBank and DocLayNet, showing that layout predictions of the DocLayNet-trained models are more robust and thus the preferred choice for general-purpose document-layout analysis.

sections.body: The introduction argues that PubLayNet and DocBank, built automatically from PubMed and arXiv sources, have limited layout variability. It presents DocLayNet, with bounding-box annotations for 11 distinct class labels on 80863 unique document pages, some carrying double or triple annotations. The stated differences from those datasets are human annotation, large layout variability, a detailed label set, redundant annotations, and pre-defined train, test and validation sets that prevent layout leakage. The section says later sections report baselines for Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN and YOLOv5, along with cross-dataset comparisons.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing layout datasets come from scientific repositories, so DocLayNet adds human-annotated pages with wider layout variety.

sections.body: Early document-layout methods used rule-based algorithms and heuristics. Recent work mostly applies object detection models, which are easy to use because of the COCO data-format standard and common frameworks such as detectron2. A newer class of models combines text tokens with the image representation of a page. The section says their reported accuracies look promising, but no broadly accepted data format linking geometric and textual features has been established yet. It contains no experiments of its own.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior layout analysis moved from rule-based methods to object detection, and newer text-plus-image models lack a shared data format.

sections.body: DocLayNet has 80863 PDF pages and 91104 annotation instances in total: 7059 pages carry two annotations and 1591 carry three. Labels are rectangular bounding boxes across 11 classes. Documents are medium to large technical files, with scanned material kept to a minimum; receipts, invoices and photographs are excluded. The six categories are Financial Reports, Manuals, Scientific Articles, Laws & Regulations, Patents and Government Tenders. Close to 95% of pages are English, with German at 2.5%, French at 1.0% and Japanese at 1.0%. Table 1 gives triple-annotator agreement of 82-83 in mAP@0.5-0.95 overall. Splits are made on full-document boundaries to avoid leakage. The section notes that language may challenge layout methods that use text features.
sections.heading: The DocLayNet Dataset
sections.headline: DocLayNet contains 80863 pages from six document categories, with 11 labels and pre-defined splits that keep documents whole.

sections.body: The campaign ran in four phases: data selection, label and guideline design, training, and production. Phases one and two used a small expert team; phases three and four used 40 annotators. In training, 974 pages were reference-annotated, and 8 of the 40 annotators did not pass the exam over 12 weeks. Production covered 80K pages handled by 32 annotators over roughly three months. The tool allowed only non-overlapping rectangular boxes, hid each annotator's work from others, and snapped boxes to text cells. Pages were rejected when no valid annotation was possible. Experienced staff took 20s to 60s per page. Some wrongly parsed PDFs had to be skipped.
sections.heading: Annotation Campaign
sections.headline: Four-phase human annotation under a guideline over 100 pages long improved consistency, though 8 of 40 annotators did not pass.

sections.body: Mask R-CNN, Faster R-CNN and YOLOv5 were trained on $1025\times 1025$ pixel images and evaluated with mAP@0.5-0.95. The text says these baselines sit between 6 and 10% below the human agreement computed on triple-annotated pages. A learning curve flattens between the 80% and 100% marks, with a 1% error-bar. Table 3 reports an overall score of 72 with 11 labels and 78 with 5 labels. Random page-wise splitting gains about 10% points over document-wise splitting, so document-wise splits are used. A Mask R-CNN R50 model trained on DocLayNet scores 78 on its test set, against 30 and 27 for PubLayNet- and DocBank-trained models on the DocLayNet test set. Only object detection methods are evaluated.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Baseline detectors trail human agreement by 6 to 10%, and random page-wise splits inflate scores by about 10%.

sections.body: The conclusion describes DocLayNet as a new, challenging dataset of human-annotated layouts, with a large share of documents outside scientific publishing. It reports human agreement from double and triple annotations, baseline object detection scores, data-size and label-set ablations, and comparisons with PubLayNet and DocBank. The authors conclude that DocLayNet-trained models transfer better to other datasets. They state that a significant gap between human and machine layout accuracy still exists and hope the work helps close it.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: DocLayNet supplies human reference metrics and models that transfer better across datasets, yet a gap to humans remains.
